Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Fast growth is easy to love and hard to value, as CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV) recently showed. On Oct. 14, 2026, the stock plunged 15% even as its revenue more than doubled, with investors worried about rising debt costs.

Image source: Getty Images.

Here's what investors are paying for growth at five fast-growing companies, ranked by the latest quarter's revenue growth: Nebius Group (NASDAQ: NBIS), CoreWeave, AppLovin (NASDAQ: APP), Robinhood Markets (NASDAQ: HOOD), and IREN (NASDAQ: IREN).

Let's start with the fastest of the bunch.

Nebius tops its AI cloud peers, but investors pay a premium

In the second quarter, revenue jumped 454% year over year to $582.3 million, outpacing neocloud rivals like Applied Digital, up 322%, and CoreWeave, up 112.5%. Nebius secured major AI cloud contracts, including agreements worth more than $1 billion each, while management has been expanding compute capacity to meet demand.

But with a price-to-sales ratio (P/S) of about 46, the highest of the five, investors are paying a hefty premium for that growth, which is largely funded by cash, customer prepayments, and outside financing.

Today's premium also rests on a long runway: management expects 5 gigawatts of contracted power by year-end and plans to add more than 1 gigawatt a year from 2027.

Nebius also faces risks around customer concentration and execution. Meanwhile, a similar company is growing fast at a more reasonable valuation.

Big AI contracts power CoreWeave's growth, but debt is a worry

CoreWeave's revenue jumped 112.5% year over year to around $2.6 billion, outpacing Google Cloud, Azure, and AWS in the same quarter. The company also reported a revenue backlog of $104 billion, and management is guiding to revenue between $12.4 and $13.2 billion this year.

The stock also trades at just 6.0 times sales, making it relatively cheaper despite its growth. But the major concern is funding: with $640 million in net interest expense, its growth relies heavily on debt, making its build-out riskier to fund.

However, unlike these high-growth neoclouds, another company is already seeing better profitability.

AppLovin's AI-driven ad business is growing and profitable

The combination of strong sales growth and profitability sets AppLovin apart from the more capital-intensive AI names.

title: Apple Joins Nvidia in the $5 Trillion Club. Here's Which Stock I Think Can Get to $10 Trillion First.
detail:
Apple Joins Nvidia in the $5 Trillion Club. Here's Which Stock I Think Can Get to $10 Trillion First.
James Brumley, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 24, 2026 at 1:37 PM EDT 4 min read
AAPL
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) was the first company to reach a $1 trillion market cap, way back in 2018. Thanks to the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence, however, hardware maker Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) became the world's first $5 trillion outfit late last year.

Now Apple's turning heads again. Thanks to its stock's recent gains, it joined the $5 trillion club just last week. Nvidia is still technically bigger, albeit barely, with its current market cap of $5.13 trillion.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

This market cap movement prompts a question: Although it doesn't really matter, which of these two companies is more likely to reach a $10 trillion valuation first? I suspect it's going to be Apple. Here's why.

Image source: Getty Images.
Apple and Nvidia are not the same

Nvidia is still a fine growth investment. Even if we don't know exactly what the future holds, we can confidently say that computing technology -- including artificial intelligence -- features prominently in it. That bodes well for this tech giant.

There's a reason NVDA shares are priced relatively cheaply at just 14 times next year's expected per-share profit of $15.91, though. That is -- perhaps without even consciously realizing it -- the market is pricing in a headwind for Nvidia's AI business. It may also be factoring in the recent rise of AI computing competitors like Advanced Micro Devices and Qualcomm. It's a potential problem because data centers alone now account for roughly 90% of Nvidia's revenue.

But isn't Apple an artificial intelligence company too? Not really. While Apple's iPhone and its iOS certainly offer artificial intelligence-based solutions to their users, these are features rather than the crux of these profit centers.

Most iPhone owners -- who consistently account for about half of Apple's sales -- simply prefer this particular smartphone for the overall experience it provides. They loved it well before AI was part of it.

And that's the key to this ticker's market-beating past, present, and projected growth. It's not a hardware company in the same sense that Nvidia provides technology to institutions that perpetually shop for the most bang for their computing buck (so to speak). Rather, Apple is a lifestyle brand that's fostered enormous loyalty from a consumer market that's already more reliable and predictable than the corporate arena.

title: Down Roughly 50% From Its Highs, Is Netflix Stock Finally a Buy?

Down Roughly 50% From Its Highs, Is Netflix Stock Finally a Buy?
Geoffrey Seiler, The Motley Fool

After hitting an all-time closing high of $133.91 on June 30, 2025, Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX) shares are down roughly 50% following the streaming giant's third-quarter earnings report. The stock's multiple compression, meanwhile, finally makes it look like a buy, despite slightly slowing revenue growth.

The video streaming company reported its third-quarter results after the closing bell on Oct. 20, which led the stock to continue its descent. The stock has been basically flat over the past five years. Let's dig into Netflix's results and prospects to see why it looks like a buy.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Making changes

It was probably pretty obvious before Netflix's report that the streaming giant wouldn't post blockbuster earnings, since it fired its chief content officer and announced its largest layoff since 2022 days before the report. It hired former Walt Disney executive Peter Rice for the role, whom the company praised for his expertise in "talent relations."

While Netflix has said its international content has been performing well, it has struggled recently to deliver big blockbuster shows in the U.S. that tend to get people talking and draw in new subscribers. In fact, there has been a narrative that the company is trying to appeal to too broad a user base (something-for-everyone shows), which has been hindering it from developing its next blockbuster. In a competitive market for talent, Netflix thinks Rice can help make it the place top creative talent wants to work with in the future.

By pivoting back to creator-friendly, quality-focused development, Netflix hopes to deliver more entertainment value to its members. It is also looking to leverage technology, continue to improve its adtech stack, and improve monetization. As such, it plans to launch ad tier subscriptions in 15 new countries next year, including nine in EMEA (Europe, the Middle East, and Africa), two in South America, and New Zealand.

For Q3, Netflix saw solid growth, with revenue increasing 12% (11% in constant currencies) to $12.87 billion. Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) surged 49% to $0.87. Analysts on average had been looking for EPS of $0.82 on revenue of $12.87 billion, according to estimates compiled by LSEG.

Revenue growth was relatively consistent across regions. U.S. and Canada revenue rose 11% to $5.6 billion, while EMEA revenue grew 11%, or 9% in constant currencies, to $4.1 billion. Latin America revenue increased by 17%, or 12% excluding currency, to $1.6 billion, while the Asia-Pacific region saw revenue rise 12%, or 15% in constant currencies, to $1.5 billion.

Bloom Energy (NYSE:BE) had lots of good news on Oct. 22. The fuel cell maker's third-quarter revenue grew 138% year over year to a record $1.24 billion, and management raised its 2026 forecast for the third time this year.

The stock still fell. Shares finished Oct. 22 at $217.77, down about 9% on the day, ahead of results released after the market closed. Then they dropped to roughly $203 in after-hours trading.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Even that $217.77 close is about 37% under the stock's record close of $345.85 on June 22.

Before the report, I said I'd look again if the new forecast put second-half revenue clearly over the second quarter's $1.07 billion. It did. Does that make the stock a buy?

Image source: Getty Images.

A third raise

Management now sees 2026 revenue landing between $4.4 billion and $4.6 billion. That compares to a July range of $3.9 billion to $4.2 billion. The forecast's low end is over double the $2.02 billion Bloom took in during 2025.

Showing how fast the company has grown, Bloom's revenue was $751 million in the first three months of 2026. It then hit $1.07 billion in the second quarter and $1.24 billion in the third. With around $3.05 billion booked through September, the latest forecast implies fourth-quarter revenue between $1.35 billion and $1.55 billion. Profits, of course, are growing even faster. Bloom's non-GAAP (adjusted) operating margin rose to 23.1% of revenue, up from 8.9% a year ago, and adjusted earnings per share climbed more than sixfold to $0.94.

The full-year profit forecast went up, too. Management now sees $3.10 to $3.40 in adjusted earnings per share, up from $2.55 to $2.85 in July.

Growth, though, is set to slow. Fourth-quarter revenue in this range would be up around 73% to 99% from the $778 million Bloom posted a year earlier. Growth like that is still strong. But it's under the 130%, 166%, and 138% growth rates for 2026's first three quarters. Some of that's a harder comparison, because Bloom's revenue climbed around 50% from the third quarter of 2025 to the fourth.

Management said the timing of a few deliveries near year-end will decide where in the range Bloom lands. For the artificial intelligence data centers it supplies, CEO KR Sridhar added that customers bring capacity online block by block, so the pace is up to them. Management also said its backlog is still growing faster than revenue, but it didn't share a new number.

title: Is Nike Still a Growth Stock? Here's the Answer.

Is Nike Still a Growth Stock? Here's the Answer.

By now, Nike (NYSE: NKE) shareholders are well aware that the company's fiscal 2027 could be a tough stretch. In the company's 2027 first-quarter earnings report, revenue fell 4% year over year to $11.2 billion, and net income slid 2% to $712 million. The athletic wear giant has been in the midst of a turnaround plan for several years now, and its first-quarter results show it's still a work in progress.

That said, aside from slumping sales and regaining relevance, Nike is also dealing with an expectation problem from the market. That's because instead of returning to growth-stock status, the iconic shoemaker may start to look more like an income stock. So, what's an investor to do?

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.
The struggles of an iconic brand

Over the years, Nike has made a series of missteps that have contributed to the stock's woes. Instead of making its products more widely available, it decided to focus more on selling directly to customers, shunning wholesalers. The brand also stagnated and felt less innovative amid a new wave of competition from brands like On Holding.

In addition, its Converse brand is struggling, with first-quarter sales of $263 million, down 28%. Even more worrisome were sales in Greater China, down 22% to $1.1 billion. On the earnings call for the quarter, CEO Elliott Hill acknowledged the company's struggles and the need to innovate, saying, "Yes, the consumer is cautious. But as the leader in the industry, it's on us to bring more creativity to sportswear."

That innovation will be important in bringing back former customers and attracting new ones, and Nike is making progress in rebuilding its wholesale pipeline. In the first quarter, sales to wholesale customers in North America totaled $2.9 billion, up 9%. For investors, however, there's an even more important element to consider before investing in Nike.

No longer a growth stock

In the fourth quarter of 2021, Nike reported revenue of $12.3 billion, a 96% increase from the prior-year period. That type of performance sets high expectations, and, looking ahead, that level of sales growth doesn't seem repeatable in the near future, nor may it ever return to that level. That said, it doesn't mean Nike can't still reward long-term investors as a more mature company.

title: Inflation Is Running Hotter Than Expected. That Could Be Bullish for Bitcoin.
detail:
Inflation Is Running Hotter Than Expected. That Could Be Bullish for Bitcoin.
Alex Carchidi, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 24, 2026 at 1:28 PM EDT 4 min read
BTC-USD
NVDA
Trade BTC on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Hot inflation could eventually help Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC), but the relationship between inflation and Bitcoin is a lot more complex than it seems. Consumer prices rose by 3.7% in the 12 months through September 2026, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), and Bitcoin fell about $1,000 on the hotter-than-expected Oct. 14 report, as hot inflation raises the odds of interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.

Still, there's an argument for why more inflation could be bullish for Bitcoin, so let's think about it a bit more.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
A digital asset can't do much about rising input costs

The Producer Price Index (PPI) is a measure of inflation that captures the prices companies receive for the goods and services they sell, before those products reach consumers; eventually, those higher costs are usually passed on to consumers in large part. Per the BLS, it jumped 1.3% in September 2026, and 6.3% over the prior 12 months. Core consumer inflation was 2.6% for the 12 months through September 2026; the Fed targets 2% on a similar gauge.

Moreover, rising energy costs probably won't ease as long as the war with Iran is ongoing. And the cost of energy is reflected in the price of almost everything else.

Bitcoin is not necessarily well suited for benefiting from any of these types of inflation.

If people's wallets are squeezed, the odds are that many of them will invest less, especially in riskier assets like Bitcoin.

Can Bitcoin hedge this inflation?

Nonetheless, Bitcoin could still benefit from inflation stemming from a different source.

J.P. Morgan Asset Management's 2027 outlook portrays Bitcoin as a bet that governments will continue to create more money, diluting the value of the existing money in circulation. Its report says that the coin typically behaves as a risky asset that tracks the global money supply. For now, the Fed is moving in the opposite direction, with markets expecting it to raise rates again before the end of the year.

On that note, new money creation is underway and is likely to continue, and probably even accelerate from here.

The M2 money supply (cash plus bank deposits) grew by 5.7% in the year through August 2026, per Federal Reserve data. If slowing economic growth in the U.S. eventually forces the Federal Reserve to make interest rate cuts while prices are still climbing, thereby making borrowing cheaper and money supply growth likelier to speed up, Bitcoin's fixed supply could serve as a refuge for those who want to hedge against inflation.

The business has quietly changed shape this year. detail:
Grayscale's New Zcash ETF Has Gathered $1 Billion in Assets in Just 30 Days. Here's Why Investors Are So Bullish on Zcash.
Lyle Daly, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 24, 2026 at 12:27 PM EDT 4 min read
ZEC-USD
ZCSH
NVDA
Trade Zcash on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Most of the major cryptocurrencies have lost value in 2026. Zcash (CRYPTO: ZEC), the largest privacy coin by market cap, is a notable exception. It's up 149% on the year as of Oct. 22.

In the midst of that bull run, asset manager Grayscale launched the Zcash ETF (NYSEMKT: ZCSH) on Aug. 25. The ETF was an immediate success, gathering more than $1 billion in its first 30 trading days. Grayscale managing director Krista Lynch noted that this puts it among the top 1% of ETFs launched over the past decade, ranked by assets gathered in the first month.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Why investors are bullish on Zcash

The main bull case for Zcash is increasing demand for financial privacy. Most types of cryptocurrency have public blockchains that provide a complete record of transactions. Zcash, on the other hand, gives users the choice between transparent and shielded addresses for each transaction. Shielded addresses encrypt the sender, receiver, amount sent, and memo field.

It anonymizes transaction data using a cryptographic method called zk-SNARKs, short for zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge. The method allows the Zcash network to mathematically verify that a transaction is valid without seeing the sender, receiver, or amount. The flexibility of Zcash sets it apart from the next-largest privacy coin, Monero, which doesn't offer transparent transactions.

About 29% of Zcash is now held in shielded addresses, up from about 12% at the start of 2025, a sign of the growing demand for privacy protection among holders.

Zcash also has the same built-in scarcity as Bitcoin, with a hard cap of 21 million ZEC, and new issuance halves roughly every four years. This scarcity will eventually eliminate inflation and could also drive up prices, assuming Zcash remains in demand.

The risks involved

The problem with privacy coins is that the feature that makes them valuable also attracts reputational issues and regulatory scrutiny. Privacy protection makes these cryptocurrencies a favorite of hackers. On-chain analysts, including ZachXBT and Specter, have reported that crypto attackers used Zcash to launder stolen funds in September and October.

Crypto exchanges have previously delisted or refused to list privacy coins, limiting trading options. Zcash is currently available on many major exchanges, including Coinbase. But that could change in the future, especially if regulators crack down on privacy coins.
